First Bet: Our Fleet or Their Servers

items: Preparation Paper — nothing is built this run

content.value: The interview demanded an honest weighing: internal fleet excellence versus a sellable agent-ready-server product, with a which-first verdict. This Paper delivers the outside-in half — twelve rivals priced, the two-vendor Claude-hosting micro-market profiled against its live pages, Anthropic's terms quoted verbatim from primary sources, the Hetzner cost floor re-measured after the June 2026 price hikes, and the community demand signal swept. The verdict:

children.value: internal-first with a named productization trigger

content.value: — not indefinite dogfooding, and not product-first. The trigger is already half-built.

Sell nothing until the fleet's two unmet root criteria — durability and the unattended mixed-agent seal — are sealed, because those are exactly the promises a paying stranger buys. But do not dogfood indefinitely: run the already-ratified pilot lane (queued early users, manual provisioning, BYO keys — PDF-D13) as a paid closed beta the moment durability seals, so the probe doubles as dogfooding. The sellable wedge is never bare “Claude on a server” — Agent 37 commoditizes that at $3.99/mo — it is the layer above: an owned box with DNS/TLS identity, a task ledger, and papers/sessions as agent memory. The trigger to flip from internal to product:

children.value: both remaining fleet criteria sealed AND pilot-lane willingness-to-pay evidence at or above the $29-plus-supports ladder.

blocks.text: The recommendation, and why each rival sequencing loses

content.value: Three independent blockers. (1) The fleet epic's unmet criteria are durability (fence-lifecycle, lease-lapse) and the unattended seal — selling now sells a promise the machinery cannot keep. (2) The one-person reality: Stripe billing is an explicit named human gate (PDS epic W4), and support/abuse/GDPR land on one founder. (3) The $3.99 anchor: a bare-hosting product fights Agent 37 on price with no moat.

The window is open NOW: Ona pivoted from CDE to agents, Agent 37 white-labels from $3.44/instance, DIY guides proliferate — demand is visible. The MVP-0 stranger journey is already sealed (6/6), so the onboarding story works today. And the internal path's real risk is scope, not sequencing: the PDS epic carries 159 children with all five root criteria still unmet. Internal-first must come with scope discipline, or it becomes internal-forever.

blocks.text: The GUI workstation market is empty in exactly our shape

content.value: The DaaS survey (Kasm ~$10/user/mo self-host; Shells Basic $9.95 → Pro $36.95-39.95 for 4 vCPU/8GB; Amazon WorkSpaces ~$25 generic; Paperspace pivoted to GPU compute; DigitalOcean has no DaaS product at all) answered the sharp question cleanly:

children.value: no vendor anywhere advertises Claude Desktop — or any AI coding agent — preinstalled on a remote Linux desktop.

content.value: The only “Claude Desktop on a VM” offer (Apps4Rent) is Windows-only and sales-assisted with no listed price; the only real preinstalled-agent cloud desktop (Windows 365 Dev Box) is Windows + Copilot. A self-serve, EUR-priced, Linux-native Claude workstation on a Hetzner cx33 (~€9.19/mo all-in) would be first to market — undercutting Shells Pro by ~4x while shipping the agent preinstalled. This is a narrow wedge in a mature desktop-hosting market, not proof the whole market is empty — but it is the strongest product-first argument found for any flavor, and it belongs to the workstation, not the headless box.

blocks.text: The ToS wall is real — and so is the BYO door through it

content.value: Primary sources, fetched raw and quoted verbatim (not tech-press paraphrase):

items.value: “Customer may not and must not attempt to (a) access the Services to build a competing product or service, including to train competing AI models or resell the Services except as expressly approved by Anthropic…” — reselling metered Claude access as a Barkpark SKU needs written approval.

“…applies to anyone who can submit inputs to Anthropic's products and/or services, including via any authorized resellers or passthrough access…” — passthrough is an anticipated, policed channel, not a loophole.

“Anthropic does not permit third-party developers to offer Claude.ai login or to route requests through Free, Pro, or Max plan credentials on behalf of their users.” And: “Advertised usage limits for Pro and Max plans assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code and the Agent SDK.”

Jan-Feb 2026 technical blocks + the Feb 20 legal clarification hit third-party harnesses (OpenClaw, OpenCode, Cline, NanoClaw confirmed named; Roo/Goose unverified). The target is tools impersonating Claude Code's auth — not the first-party CLI run by its owner.

content.value: “We preinstall the CLI on a box we rent you; you log in with your own credentials” touches neither D.4 (only compute is sold, not the Services) nor the OAuth ban (Barkpark never sits in the auth path). The crux is whether Barkpark ever stores, proxies, or vends Anthropic credentials on the user's behalf — that crossing is what turns a compliant preinstall into prohibited passthrough. The safest sellable framing:

children.value: rented compute with Claude Code preinstalled; you authenticate directly with Anthropic.

content.value: No primary source explicitly blesses this model — it is an inference from what the clauses do and do not prohibit, and Anthropic “reserves the right to take measures… without prior notice.”

blocks.title: The legal reading the strategy hangs on — flagged as inference

content.value: Consumer-side constraints that bound the economics: Max 5x is $100/mo, Max 20x $200/mo, but Anthropic no longer publishes fixed hours-per-week — the widely quoted figures are third-party estimates. “Ordinary, individual usage” argues directly against one Max seat backing multiple always-on fleet workers; concurrent-device limits are undocumented (contractually ambiguous, not permitted-by-silence). Any crossover model between subscription and API-key economics must carry both caveats — and Anthropic can retune the underlying pools silently.

(cache writes ~59% of agent cost), so box margin is not the business; the BYO posture is what makes $29 mostly margin.

blocks.text: Risks & unknowns
Risks the recommendation carries

items.value: No Anthropic document blesses rent-a-box-BYO-login; enforcement can arrive “without prior notice.” Mitigation: the BYO posture keeps Barkpark out of the auth path entirely; re-check the legal-and-compliance page each wave.

Internal-first can arrive after buyers settle on Agent 37/Ona-class incumbents. Mitigation: the trigger is evidence-gated, not calendar-gated — and the GUI workstation gap is currently uncontested, buying time.
The internal path has historically expanded scope (159-child epic, root unsealed). Naming the trigger converts “later” into a checkable predicate — but only if the capstone ratifies it as law.
Even a successful closed beta lands support, abuse, and GDPR (German boxes) on one founder while Wave D builds.

The 12-vendor prices are aggregator-sourced; Anthropic's subscription limits are unpublished and silently tunable; Hetzner repriced twice in six months. Every number here has a stated grade — quote accordingly.
All unit economics are modeled. Spend telemetry must land before pilot pricing is honest.

Risks & unknowns

Risks the recommendation carries

  • The ToS reading is inference. No Anthropic document blesses rent-a-box-BYO-login; enforcement can arrive “without prior notice.” Mitigation: the BYO posture keeps Barkpark out of the auth path entirely; re-check the legal-and-compliance page each wave.
  • Market-window risk. Internal-first can arrive after buyers settle on Agent 37/Ona-class incumbents. Mitigation: the trigger is evidence-gated, not calendar-gated — and the GUI workstation gap is currently uncontested, buying time.
  • Scope-discipline risk. The internal path has historically expanded scope (159-child epic, root unsealed). Naming the trigger converts “later” into a checkable predicate — but only if the capstone ratifies it as law.
  • One-person absorption risk. Even a successful closed beta lands support, abuse, and GDPR (German boxes) on one founder while Wave D builds.
  • Evidence-grade risk. The 12-vendor prices are aggregator-sourced; Anthropic's subscription limits are unpublished and silently tunable; Hetzner repriced twice in six months. Every number here has a stated grade — quote accordingly.
  • No measured spend. All unit economics are modeled. Spend telemetry must land before pilot pricing is honest.

Judgment calls explicitly left to the user

  1. Which sellable unit leads when the trigger fires: fleet-support attach (this lane's recommendation), GUI workstation, or standalone VPS — taste and appetite, not a fetchable fact.
  2. How real and how large is the “queued early users” pilot lane the MVP paper claims — a count and profiles are user truth only you can supply; the pilot design depends on it.
  3. Is dual-track structurally impossible or merely expensive — i.e., how much founder attention exists to split.
  4. Whether the 7x price story (knowledge system over compute) deserves a pre-pilot perception test, or whether the pilot itself is the test.
  5. If metered pass-through is ever wanted: Bedrock/Vertex routing vs. a direct Anthropic arrangement under D.4's express-approval clause — the go/no-go is a business judgment.
  6. Whether to amend D62 toward automated credential delivery (ClawHosters-style vault) — the owner sign-off gate PDF-D88 already names.
